summary.text: 働 is a Japanese-created character meaning “work,” read hataraku. It combines the person component 亻 with 動, “move.” 動 also links it with the reading dō. The construction is more informative than “a person moving”: it connects a human activity with an existing character used for movement.

formation.text: 亻 supplies a human meaning component, while 動 is associated with both movement and pronunciation. Whether the combined meaning directly motivated the coinage is disputed.

components.text: 亻 is the normal left-side form of 人, “person.” It marks the human activity in 働.
動 is kept as a whole component. It supplies the dō sound link and the movement association; one historical account instead emphasizes its pre-existing use to write hataraku.

sound.text: 動 and 働 share the on’yomi dō. The native Japanese reading hataraku is a separate kun’yomi; it is not derived from the sound dō.

history.text: One account traces 働 to adding 人 to 動 when 動 could already be read hataraku, distinguishing that use from ugoku, “move.” Another explains the formation through the combined meaning of person and movement as well as sound. Both identify the same written parts, but differ about why the added person component was needed.
Chinese later borrowed the Japanese written character and assigned it the pronunciation of 動, dòng. That borrowing is a separate event from the character’s creation in Japan.

uncertainties.text: The disagreement concerns the circumstances of formation, not whether 亻 and 動 are present. A person in motion remains an intelligible meaning association, but should not be presented as a settled reconstruction of the original coinage.

evidence.text:
Orthographic borrowing from Japanese 働.
Spelling pronunciation as 動 /动 (dòng).
The legs of a human being
Pictograph of the side view of a person.
天地之性最貴者也。此籒文。象臂脛之形。凡人之屬皆从人。

Pictogram (象形) – side view of a standing man, highlighting an arm and a leg. Compare 大, 立 (lì), 卩, 夭, and 氏 according to one interpretation. See also the original version of 年.
亼 is similar but unrelated; it represents an open mouth flipped upside down and appears on top of characters such as 食, 金, 令, 龠, and 今.
It represents a roof in the characters 余, 茶, 舍, and 倉. It represents a flag on a flagpole in 㫃. Eventually, it represents two parallel mountain walls in 谷.
The stylized version to the left of the characters is 亻 (see also 千). Similar but unrelated to 彳.
Sagart (1999) relates it to Tibetan ཉེན (nyen, “relative”), from ཉེ (nye, “near”) + nominalizing suffix -n; if so, from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *nəj(ʔ) (“near”).
Schuessler (2007) proposes two etymologies:
* Same etymon as 仁 (OC *njin, “to be kind; to be good”), from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s/k-niŋ (“heart; brain; mind”). The semantic association of 仁 with 人 was somewhat late, dated to Mencius's time; later on, 仁 would be usually interpreted as "humane, acting like a human being".
** If so, semantically parallel with Tibetan སེམས་ཅན (sems can, “living being, human, animal”, literally “possessor of mind”); and Latin animalis (“living, having soul”) from anima (“soul”).
* Related to Proto-Mon-Khmer *ɲaʔ ~ *ɲah (“person”) with a nominalizing suffix -n, from the auto-ethnonym of a hostile, possibly Austroasiatic-speaking, eastern people, whom the Sinitic-speaking Shang referred to as 人方 (OC *njin paŋ).

The Min native word for “person”; used as a replacement character for 儂 /侬. It is historically attested for Hokkien in the Arte de la Lengua Chiõ Chiu (1620) and Dictionario Hispanico Sinicum (1626-1642). Use of 人 for Hokkien is recommended by Taiwan's Ministry of Education (ROC MOE).
天地之性最貴者也。此籒文。象臂脛之形。凡人之屬皆从人。
Phonosemantic compound. 力 represents the meaning and 重 represents the sound.

Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *doːŋʔ): phonetic 重 (OC *doŋ, *doŋʔ, *doŋs) + semantic 力 (“strength”). However, the phonetic component is a reference to a heavy bag ready to be moved by a human being.
A Japanese-created character meaning work, with readings hataraku and dō. Its formation is classed as combining meaning and sound: person plus 動, movement, pronounced dō.
evidence.title: 働 — formation, meanings and readings

evidence.text: A competing historical account says 動 already wrote hataraku and 人 was added to distinguish this use from ugoku. It analyzes 動 as phonetic and rejects a newly invented person-plus-movement story, citing Sasahara 2024 and the Unpo Irohashū.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.
